readings.title: Studying between shifts
readings.instruction: Read the original simulation passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: Dale worked alternating early and late shifts while taking an evening accounting course. He first planned to study at the same hour every day, but his rota made that impossible. His tutor suggested choosing three short study periods after the rota arrived each week. Dale also wrote down one specific task for each period, such as explaining an example without notes. He missed fewer sessions, although progress remained slow during busy weeks. He no longer measured commitment by having an identical daily routine. The course still required effort; the new plan simply fitted the circumstances in which that effort was possible.
knowledgePoints: 阅读：主旨、细节、推断与语境词义

readings.title: Why the recording was not enough
readings.instruction: Read the original simulation passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: Harbour College recorded lectures for students who could not always attend. After several weeks, tutors noticed that some students watched a recording repeatedly but still struggled with related problems. One tutor inserted pauses with a question to answer before continuing. Students could compare their response with a later explanation. Many said the pauses revealed what they had not understood. The college did not require everyone to watch at one speed or one time. It treated the recording as a resource for active work rather than as a complete substitute for thinking through a problem.

readings.title: A quiet room at lunchtime
readings.instruction: Read the original simulation passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: A factory offered its meeting room to employees who wanted to read at lunch. The room was usually quiet, but a sign saying 'Study Room' discouraged workers who only wanted to practise a few words or read a manual. After a discussion, the sign was changed to 'Learning Break: All Welcome'. A volunteer also explained that attendance created no obligation to join a course. More employees began visiting. The room could still be booked for essential meetings, so the weekly availability was posted near the entrance. The experiment showed that an invitation could matter as much as a physical space.
knowledgePoints: 阅读：主旨、细节、推断与语境词义

readings.title: The notebook of errors
readings.instruction: Read the original simulation passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: When Mei returned to mathematics, she felt discouraged by the red marks on her exercises. A classmate suggested keeping an error notebook. For each difficult problem, Mei recorded the mistaken step, the reason it seemed reasonable, and a corrected example. She reviewed a few entries before starting new work. The notebook did not eliminate mistakes, and copying every incorrect answer would have taken too long. Mei selected errors that revealed a repeated misunderstanding. Over time she became better at noticing the point where her reasoning changed direction. Errors became information she could use rather than a simple count of failure.
knowledgePoints: 阅读：主旨、细节、推断与语境词义

translation.stem:
Translate the following original passage into Chinese. Preserve the meaning and logical relationships.

Returning to education does not mean starting life again. Adults bring useful experience to the classroom, even when they have forgotten some school knowledge. A flexible timetable can help them continue studying. Equally important is the confidence to ask questions without feeling embarrassed.
translation.referenceAnswer: 重返校园并不意味着重新开始人生。成年人即使遗忘了一些学校知识，也能把有用的经验带进课堂。灵活的时间安排有助于他们坚持学习。同样重要的是，他们能够自信地提问，而不感到尴尬。
translation.explanation: 参考译文仅示范一种表达。评分时关注信息完整性、转折和条件等逻辑关系；意思准确且中文自然的其他译法同样有效。

writing.stem:
Write an English response of about 120 words to the following original simulation task. Use your own examples and organise your ideas clearly.

Write to an adult education tutor proposing a study group for shift workers. Describe scheduling difficulties and suggest two arrangements.
writing.sampleAnswer: Dear Tutor, Several members of our class work changing shifts, and we would like to form a study group. A fixed meeting every Tuesday would exclude some of us in alternate weeks. Could we arrange two short sessions covering the same topic, with each learner attending whichever fits their rota? We could share a brief written summary afterwards. I also suggest choosing a weekly practice task in advance, so that anyone who misses both sessions can still contribute a question or an answer. The group should support the course rather than create another heavy obligation. I would be happy to collect members' available times and prepare a first schedule. Yours sincerely, A class member
